turn_text: After that bill passed the House, it was time for the Senate to rewrite its own version. The Senate is not a majoritarian institution. I would think these two observations would be fairly obvious to even a casual observer of the United States Congress. So I had hopes that we could end up going to conference I found out that that wasn't going to happen. That was frustrating, not just for me. I mean, again, I lead a band of men and women of great privilege to lead them, and they had many different bills, that many of which were not particularly controversial. that were left on the Senate cutting room floor. That should have been in any negotiation or any conference. We were displeased with the way the Senate handled this, but at the end of the day, they did come up with something. As you know, in order to, it was never a question of whether or not we would have a deregulation, a deregulatory banking bill. The only thing that was in question was what was its precise timing in this Congress and how robust would it be? So after some negotiations and meetings with my membership, we did decide that we would let 2155 proceed. turn_text: You recently said in an interview at the American Enterprise Institute, and I'm going to quote you here, between trying to get rid of the farm program, trying to get rid of vaccine, trying to get rid of the GSEs, I've taken on a lot of very, very tough causes. What would you say to maybe some critics in both parties who might argue that it may have been more productive to sort of push more compromised bills through the house?

Well, again, I think we can do both. I think one, you have to fight for your vision, you have to fight for your principles, but that doesn't prevent you from acting incrementally. I think by just about any measure whatsoever, you will find the financial services committee to have been among the most productive, if not the most productive committee in Congress. When you measure us by the number of bills that we passed out of committee, bills passed on the floor, bills signed into law, number of hearings, number of markups. I think by that lens, by that measurement, you will find us an incredibly productive committee and you will also find most of our measures, not all. Most of our measures passed on a bipartisan basis, many on a strongly bipartisan basis. But simply because I work for incremental change doesn't mean that my principles have changed and it doesn't change what is right and what is wrong and what helps working men and women, what lifts people from property, what helps create modern economic growth, what helps people get into houses, what helps people start small businesses. So I think those are very, very important battles to have. And to me, capitalism is one of the great forces of good in the history of mankind. It is clearly, again, help people get into homes that otherwise would not help homes. It helps people have nutritional meals, who otherwise wouldn't have nutritional meals. It helps people start their own business, who otherwise would be an employment of others. It helps people sleep at night, not having to worry whether or not there's enough money tomorrow to buy groceries and to pay the drugist bill. I never want anybody to confuse capitalism with crony capitalism. because it confuses people. It besmirches the reputation and integrity of the greatest housing, nutritional, and education program devised by the mind of man, and that is free enterprise, a system that has never been enjoyed more robustly than in America. But I fear that subsidies and set aside in earmarks And special interests can undermine that system. And I think we see vestiges of it today. And at the end of the day, conservatives will never be able, never be able to reform welfare as long as our hands are unclean with respect to corporate welfare. and you cannot take America off the road to bankruptcy unless ultimately you reform current entitlement programs for future generations.

turn_text: One of the areas where you've recently shown compromise is with housing finance reform. You have this bill, uh, reforming Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac. Uh, you have a package with Democratic representatives, John Delaney and Jim Himes, and I imagine others. Why is now the time for this negotiation?

Well, why not today? I mean, I can do it tomorrow. I can do it yesterday. I can do it today. So I'm getting ready to leave Congress, as you know, otherwise we wouldn't be having this interview. I would say if you had a couple of hours, I could go through my list of disappointments in serving in Congress for 16 years. Probably the biggest disappointment I have is that I was not able to get signed into law a comprehensive housing finance reform bill. I think a government guarantee in the secondary mortgage market is not necessary and it's very risky. Having fought it for a number of years, I sense that it is going to be a longstanding feature of our housing finance system. So if we're going to have it, and if there's going to be some kind of compromise, I'm worried about the status quo. I'm worried about the status quo because I think that risk or building up in the system yet again, I fear we are repeating many of the same mistakes that brought us to the crisis in the first place. So again, I don't want there to be a government guarantee, but if there is going to be one, We at least need elements of competition, innovation, risk dispersion, and put the taxpayer in a catastrophic loss position only, which is what I think you saw the work that has taken many, many months to get here to have, at least on the house side, a bipartisan, comprehensive bill. So I'm under no illusions that this is going to get signed into law in this Congress. It is my intention to take this as far as it can be taken in this Congress.
